analysis.one_liner: Lifts major campaign contribution limits and lets corporations, unions, and big donors spend more on federal elections.
analysis.headline: A House committee reported the bill 6-3 and put it on the House calendar in June 2005, but it never got a floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo key limits from the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. It would erase the overall cap on what any one individual can donate across a two-year cycle, lift the cap on how much party committees can spend coordinated with candidates, and raise PAC contribution limits. It would also let corporations, trade associations, and unions fund broadcast ads targeting candidates, let state parties spend unregulated 'soft money' on voter registration, and exempt the internet from campaign finance rules. A few provisions went the other way, barring foreign money from 527 groups and requiring those groups to report to the FEC.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy individual donors, who could give to unlimited numbers of candidates and party committees once the aggregate cap disappears [S3][S4]; national party committees, which could make unlimited coordinated general-election spending on behalf of candidates [S3][S4]; corporations, trade associations, and labor unions, which could fund targeted electioneering ads and solicit PAC money from members by email and fax rather than only by mail [S3][S4]; and leadership PACs run by sitting members of Congress, which could transfer money to national party committees outside the usual limits [S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy donors, party committees, big corporations

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the aggregate limit on individual contributions, so one donor could give the maximum to every candidate, party, and PAC without a yearly cap [S2][S3][S4]
Repeals the cap on coordinated party spending in general elections, letting national parties spend any amount on behalf of their candidates [S3][S4]
Repeals the 'Wellstone Amendment,' letting civic groups, trade associations, and labor organizations pay for targeted electioneering communications [S3][S4]
Raises PAC contribution limits from $5,000 to $7,500 and PAC-to-party limits from $15,000 to $25,000, and indexes most limits to inflation [S3][S4]
Lets state and local parties spend nonfederal 'soft money' on voter registration and sample ballots, and exempts internet communications from campaign finance regulation [S3][S4]
Adds some regulation: bans foreign nationals from giving to 527 organizations and requires 527 groups to file FEC reports on the same schedule as political committees [S3][S4]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters, who would face elections financed by larger checks from a smaller set of donors, parties, and corporate and union treasuries; the bill also raises the threshold at which a political group must register with the FEC from $1,000 to $10,000 per year, removing public reporting for smaller political operations [S3][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters facing costlier, less transparent elections

drawbacks.text: Raising the political committee registration threshold from $1,000 to $10,000 would let small political groups raise and spend money without registering or reporting to the FEC [S3][S4]
Exempting internet communications from the definition of 'public communication' would leave paid online political advertising outside campaign finance rules [S3][S4]
Repealing the aggregate individual cap and the party coordinated spending cap would concentrate influence in the hands of the largest donors and the national parties [S3][S4]

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: the 2002 law's limits can burden grassroots advocacy and nonprofit speech, and the bill did add real safeguards, including a foreign-money ban and FEC reporting for 527 groups [S3][S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill included a few genuine transparency and anti-foreign-money provisions, but its dominant effect was to raise the ceiling on big money in federal elections: unlimited individual giving, unlimited coordinated party spending, and corporate and union treasury-funded attack ads. For a reader who cares about the price of influencing Congress, the costs outweigh the modest transparency additions.

outcome.mechanism: The House Administration Committee approved it 6-3 and put it on the House calendar in June 2005, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Pence introduced the bill on March 15, 2005, joined by Rep. Albert Wynn as the bill's Democratic co-lead [S4][S6]
It was referred to the Committee on House Administration, which marked it up on June 8 and ordered it reported on a 6-3 vote [S6]
The committee reported the bill with amendments on June 22, 2005, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills ready for House floor consideration [S1][S6]
No further action followed: the bill never received a floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S6]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the campaign finance limits in place under the 2002 McCain-Feingold law, since those limits stayed in force — and, by extension, voters were spared a rollback of contribution caps. The bill's backers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Backers of existing campaign finance limits

for.name: Rep. Mike Pence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave introductory remarks on the House floor three times, and saw it reported from committee

for.name: Rep. Albert Wynn
for.what_they_did: Joined Pence in introducing the bill, giving it a bipartisan face

for.name: House Administration Committee Republicans
for.role: Committee majority that controlled the markup
for.what_they_did: Approved the bill 6-3 in markup and reported it to the House floor calendar

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leaders who control the House floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote; it sat on the Union Calendar for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Campaign finance reform groups
against.role: Outside advocacy organizations such as Public Citizen and Democracy 21
against.what_they_did: Opposed rolling back the 2002 McCain-Feingold limits and the loosening of corporate and union spending rules

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily one-party: 38 cosponsors split 37 Republicans and 1 Democrat, and the committee approved it 6-3, with the majority party's members carrying it and no record of floor action.

industries.note: The bill would let parties make unlimited coordinated spending on behalf of general-election candidates and let state parties spend soft money on registration drives. Parties would gain fund-raising and spending power at the expense of contribution limits voters have lived under since 2002.
Repealing the aggregate contribution cap would let a single donor give the maximum to unlimited candidates, parties, and PACs. Candidates would owe even more to a small donor class.

Repealing the Wellstone Amendment would let corporate and trade-association organizations fund targeted electioneering ads, and the bill would free their PACs to solicit employees by email and fax with fewer restrictions. This widens the channel for corporate money into elections.

industries.industry: Leadership PACs run by sitting members of Congress
industries.note: The bill would exempt transfers from lawmakers' leadership committees to national party committees from contribution limits, letting officeholders move money to the parties outside the usual caps.

Unions, like corporations, would regain the ability to fund targeted electioneering communications and solicit members by any communication method rather than only mail. The gain mirrors the corporate one but operates from a smaller member base.
Unlimited coordinated party spending and reopened electioneering ads would increase total spending on political media. Consultants and ad buyers would capture more of the money raised.
